content: Citrate is the ionic form of citric acid, represented as C₃H₅O(COO)₃³⁻, which is essentially citric acid with three hydrogen ions removed. Citrates are compounds that contain the citrate group. These can be ionic compounds, such as salts, or covalent compounds, such as esters. For example, sodium citrate is a salt, while trimethyl citrate is an ester. Citric acid, being a multifunctional acid, can form intermediate ions such as the hydrogen citrate ion (HC₆H₅O₇²⁻) and the dihydrogen citrate ion (H₂C₆H₅O₇⁻). These ions can also form salts, which are referred to as acid salts. Salts of the hydrogen citrate ions are weakly acidic, whereas salts of the citrate ion itself, when paired with an inert cation like sodium, are weakly basic. Citrate plays a critical role in buffering systems, such as the SSC 20X hybridization buffer. A 3M sodium citrate solution is typically titrated with NaOH to achieve a pH of 7. However, when the components are mixed, the pH tends to be slightly basic, necessitating further titration with HCl to bring the pH back to 7. Additionally, citric acid can function as a mild chelating agent. Citrate is a key intermediate in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, also known as the Krebs cycle. After the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA using five cofactors (thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoamide, FAD, NAD⁺, and CoA), citrate synthase catalyzes the condensation of oxaloacetate with acetyl-CoA to form citrate. Citrate then progresses through the TCA cycle via aconitase, ultimately regenerating oxaloacetate, which can combine with another acetyl-CoA molecule to continue the cycle. In glycolysis, high concentrations of citrate can inhibit phosphofructokinase, the rate-limiting enzyme of the glycolytic pathway.
